title: Equipment pulse recorder
subtitle: Speed and stall monitoring with bounded interrupt work
problem: A lab operator needs speed, running-time estimates and a clear stalled indication from a low-voltage fan or test fixture. This recorder counts digital pulses, reports speed at 100 ms intervals and lights an LED after two seconds without a pulse. It is a monitor, not a machine safety controller.
summary: A rising edge interrupts the processor briefly. The interrupt accepts an edge only if it is far enough from the previous accepted edge, then updates a count and timestamp. Every 100 ms the task snapshots that shared state. Speed is the count difference divided by actual elapsed time and pulses per revolution. A saturating idle timer prevents a stopped machine from appearing active when the microsecond clock wraps.
requirements: GPIO27; <=1 kHz; reject edges <500 us; short ISR
Debounce model passes; real pulse fidelity pending
Counter/time wrap and stall simulation pass
ADC1 GPIO34 raw samples; LED GPIO25
p99 report jitter <5 ms; 5 s watchdog
bom: 10 kohm pot, LED, 1 kohm resistors, wires
decisions: The ISR uses the ESP timer timestamp and a critical section around its counter/timestamps. Its debounce timestamp is 64-bit to avoid rejecting a first pulse after a very long idle because of 32-bit aliasing. The reporting task takes the same lock only while copying fields; formatting and ADC reads happen outside it.

Speed uses modular count difference and actual elapsed microseconds. The calculation assumes snapshots occur more frequently than one 32-bit timer wrap, which is satisfied by the 100 ms target. The 1 kHz limit also prevents ambiguity from a full count wrap between reports.

Idle age accumulates between snapshots and saturates at two seconds. A changed count resets age from the latest edge. Once stalled, the output remains stalled until a new pulse is observed, even through repeated microsecond timer wraps.

PPR changes are parsed from a 32-byte bounded line, constrained to 1..32, CRC-sealed and committed to NVS before replacing the live value. Writes are rate-limited to once per second. A PPR change applies at the next report and may affect that boundary interval; perform calibration while stopped.

Runtime is accumulated for reporting intervals whose latest pulse is within the stall timeout. It includes the timeout tail, and is not exact shaft-on time. ADC1 avoids the ADC2/radio restriction but is still uncalibrated; output is raw ADC counts, never fabricated volts.
tests: 500 us debounce boundary and wrapped timestamps
Counter rollover, elapsed rollover, zero interval, no-pulse startup
90,000 reports covering two timer wraps while stopped
Invalid numbers, oversized commands, config corruption and reload

Real pulse capture, ADC linearity, ISR latency, watchdog, NVS power cut
failures: The first long-idle regression failed: direct subtraction from an old edge made the stopped device appear recently active after a timer wrap. A saturating idle-age accumulator fixed it; 90,000 report intervals now cover more than two wraps. Review also changed the ISR debounce timestamp to 64-bit. The model and physical adapter timing remain separately identified.
limitations: Speed is quantized by pulses per reporting window, especially at low RPM. The synthetic jitter test uses pulse counts that divide cleanly into its intervals; real edge phase adds quantization. Debounce can reject legitimate pulses closer than 500 microseconds, so the supported rate is deliberately limited to 1 kHz. Runtime includes a timeout tail. The LED is not a safety output. ADC voltage and sample timing require calibration and measurement.
experiments: Drive GPIO27 with 10, 100 and 1000 Hz 3.3 V square waves for 60 s each. Compare accepted counts with a generator or logic analyzer. Add narrow bounce pulses <500 microseconds and confirm rejection without suppressing valid edges.

Capture a diagnostic GPIO toggled at each report along with the input pulses for 10 minutes. Compute actual interval p50/p95/p99 and missed periods; target p99 jitter <5 ms. Stop pulses at randomized phases and verify LED latency <=2.1 s.

Change PPR while stopped, reboot and verify persistence; cut power during configuration writes. Compare ADC raw counts at measured 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 V inputs. Disable watchdog feeding in a temporary test build and verify reset.

questions: Why use actual elapsed time?
A task may run early or late. Dividing counts by an assumed 100 ms produces a speed error proportional to interval error.
Why does unsigned subtraction handle rollover?
Arithmetic is modulo 2^32. If the actual elapsed interval is less than one wrap, now minus then gives that interval even when the counter crossed zero.
Why was subtraction alone insufficient for stall detection?
The last edge can be older than a complete wrap. Its modular age then looks small again. Saturating accumulated idle age avoids that ambiguity.
Does volatile make shared data safe?
No. It prevents certain compiler assumptions but does not make a multi-field snapshot atomic. The ISR and task use the same critical-section lock.
What limits the maximum input frequency?
Debounce rejects edges closer than 500 microseconds, and ISR service also consumes time. The design targets 1 kHz and requires physical verification.
What does PPR mean?
Pulses per revolution. RPM equals pulses per second times 60 divided by PPR. A wrong PPR produces a proportional calibration error.
Why does low-speed RPM jump?
A short window may contain zero or one pulse. Period measurement or adaptive windows can improve low-speed resolution at the cost of response behavior.
Why is runtime approximate?
The state remains active until the two-second stall timeout and updates in reporting intervals. The metric includes that tail and boundary quantization.
What is the ADC measuring?
Only raw counts from a 0-3.3 V test input. Reference variation and nonlinearity mean a voltage claim needs calibration.
How would you improve the hardware?
Use the ESP32 pulse-counter peripheral for higher rates, an appropriate input protection/level interface, and physical timing tests. Compare PCNT and ISR results before claiming improvement.
